title: Splitting Analysis for Yukawa Potential
abstract: Splitting methods are among the most classical and fundamental tools for the simulation of quantum dynamics, and their importance has grown further with the rise of quantum computing. In this work, we analyze the Schrödinger equation with Yukawa potential, a physically relevant and widely used model potential. It may be viewed as a Coulomb interaction with exponential decay at spatial infinity, preserving the Coulomb singularity at the origin while removing the long-range Coulomb tail. We prove that the operator splitting for this unbounded Hamiltonian achieves a global $1/4$-order convergence rate in the time step for many-body Yukawa interactions, with explicit polynomial dependence on the number of particles. The result holds for all initial wavefunctions in $H^2(\mathbb R^{3N})$, the natural domain of the Hamiltonian, and our numerical experiments are consistent with the theoretical estimates. To identify the sharp obstruction behind this rate, we prove a short-time lower bound in the one-body setting of order $t^{5/4}$ for the one-step error, which rules out any uniform global estimate of order better than $1/4$ in general. This agreement with the optimal $1/4$ rate in the Coulomb case is particularly interesting, as Yukawa potential is short-ranged compared to Coulomb potential. For the many-body upper bound, one of the new technical ingredients is the explicit polynomial-in-system-size Sobolev estimates of many-body Yukawa systems. These estimates are crucial for obtaining fully a priori bounds that depend only on the norms of the initial states, rather than on the solution at time $t$. For the one-body lower bound, we leverage a new analysis argument based on Fourier analysis and Kato smoothing.
summary: This paper rigorously analyzes the error convergence of splitting methods applied to simulate quantum dynamics with a Yukawa potential. It proves that the simulation achieves an optimal global time-step convergence rate of $O(t^{1/4})$ by establishing both upper and lower bounds. The work is significant for providing mathematically rigorous tools for simulating many-body systems where interactions are short-ranged but singular at the origin.
main_problem: The paper analyzes the convergence rate of splitting methods used to simulate quantum dynamics governed by the Schrödinger equation with a Yukawa potential.
main_result: It proves a global O(t^1/4) convergence rate for many-body interactions, establishing this rate as sharp by deriving a corresponding lower bound. The result shows that the short-range nature of the Yukawa potential does not improve upon the leading error obstruction dictated by the origin singularity.
method: The analysis employs rigorous mathematical techniques including Sobolev estimates, Fourier analysis, and Kato smoothing to derive both upper (convergence) and lower bounds on the time evolution error.
model_or_system: The system is a many-body quantum mechanical model described by the Schrödinger equation with a Yukawa potential, which acts as a screened Coulomb interaction. The Hamiltonian is $H_\mu = -\Delta + V_\mu$, where $V_\mu$ decays exponentially at large distances.
key_observables: The primary observable is the error norm $\left\|U_{1,\mu}(t)^L\psi_0 - e^{-iT}H_\mu\psi_0ight\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^{3N})}$, which measures the difference between the numerical approximation and the exact evolution.
important_parameters: The key parameters are the time step ($\Delta t$ or $t$), the total time ($T$), the number of particles ($N$), and the screening parameter ($\mu$) defining the potential range.
main_assumptions: The analysis requires working in strong norms, specifically the $H^2(\mathbb{R}^{3N})$ domain, due to the unbounded kinetic energy and singular nature of the potential at the origin.
paper_structure: The paper builds from establishing the physical model (Yukawa potential) to developing rigorous error estimates. It first proves an upper bound on the splitting error, leveraging novel system-size Sobolev estimates. Subsequently, it establishes a matching lower bound using Fourier analysis and Kato smoothing to prove the rate is optimal.
why_interesting: This work provides highly technical convergence guarantees for simulating complex quantum many-body systems, which directly informs the development of stable and efficient numerical algorithms for condensed matter simulations.
